z-m-10-01.title: Checking the angle between clock hands that Hajun found
z-m-10-01.topic: The angle formed by the two hands of a clock
z-m-10-01.goal: In a solution that found the angle formed by the two clock hands, find and fix the line whose reasoning doesn't hold (where the movement of the hour hand was missed), and use the same idea to find acute-angle times yourself and explain why.
z-m-10-01.material:
On a clock face, the numbers 1 to 12 are placed at equal spacing. One full turn is 360°, so the angle between one number and the next is 30°. The short hand (hour hand) moves at a steady speed of one number space (30°) per hour, and the long hand (minute hand) points at the number 6 at 30 minutes. The angle between the two hands means the angle on the side that is not greater than 180°. No picture is shown, so picture the clock face in your mind.
Hajun found the angle between the two hands at 2:30 as below.
z-m-10-01.thinking.0: Finding the error by checking which time each line of the solution is talking about
z-m-10-01.thinking.1: Making and comparing examples by changing conditions
z-m-10-01.prereq.0: One full turn is 360°, and the clock face is divided equally into 12 spaces, so one number space is 30°
z-m-10-01.prereq.1: Reading the size of angles and the meaning of acute, obtuse, and right angles (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Hajun's solution whose reasoning doesn't hold.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.0: Sort out one by one whether each line talks about the clock at exactly 2 o'clock or at 2:30.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.1: Picture side by side where the hour hand points at exactly 2 o'clock and exactly 3 o'clock, and think where it would be at 2:30, which is between them.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.line.0: At 30 minutes, the long hand points at the number 6.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.line.1: At exactly 2 o'clock, the hour hand points at the number 2.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.line.2: So at 2:30 too, the hour hand is still at the number 2.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.line.3: From the number 2 to 6 is 4 spaces and one space is 30°, so 4×30=120°.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.line.4: So the angle between the two hands is 120°.
z-m-10-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 doesn't hold. The hour hand moves one space (30°) steadily per hour, so at 2:30 it has gone another half space (15°) past the number 2 and is exactly halfway between 2 and 3. Then from the hour hand to the number 6 is 3 and a half spaces, which is 3.5×30=105°. Line 1 is right for the long hand's position at 30 minutes, and line 2 is right because it is the picture of "exactly 2 o'clock". The calculation on line 4 is right by itself but it used the wrong position from line 3, and line 5 is the result of that.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.prompt: Think the same way and, at the half hour (from 1:30 to 11:30), find three different times when the angle between the two hands is an acute angle (an angle less than 90°). The angle between the two hands is the angle on the side not greater than 180°. Write only the "hour" of which hour and 30 minutes.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.0: At 30 minutes, the long hand is always at the number 6. Pick a time and write which two numbers the hour hand is between.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare, at several times, how many spaces the hour hand is from the number 6, and measure that against the number of spaces that equals 90°.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.var.h: The 'hour' of which hour and 30 minutes (1 to 11)
z-m-10-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the hour as a natural number from 1 to 11.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The angle between the two hands is an acute angle, less than 90°.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time, the angle between the two hands is not less than 90°. Count the spaces between where the hour hand is at that time and the number 6.
z-m-10-01.s.s2.explain: From 3:30 to 8:30, all are acute angles. For example, at 4:30 the hour hand is exactly halfway between 4 and 5 (135°) and the long hand is at 6 (180°), so the angle between the hands is 45°. 1:30 (135°), 2:30 (105°), 9:30 (105°), 10:30 (135°), and 11:30 (165°) are greater than 90°.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.prompt: At 1:30 or 10:30 the angle between the two hands is not an acute angle, and from 3:30 to 8:30 it is an acute angle. Use the position of the hour hand to write why.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write which two numbers the hour hand is between at 3:30 and at 10:30.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether that position is close to or far from the number 6.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., At 1:30, the hour hand is ...
z-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say in your writing which numbers the hour hand is between?
z-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use whether that position is close to or far from the number 6 as your reason?
z-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you connect it to the standard "acute angle" or "90°"?
z-m-10-01.s.s3.model.0: At 1:30 the hour hand is between 1 and 2, so it is far from the number 6. So the angle between the two hands is 135°, an obtuse angle greater than 90°.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.model.1: If the hour hand is more than three spaces away from the number 6, the angle is wider than 90°. At 10:30 the hour hand is between 10 and 11, so it is four and a half spaces away from 6, and it is not an acute angle.
z-m-10-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer explained by the number of spaces is good too.

z-m-10-02.title: When shapes meet at one point, will a gap remain or will they overlap?
z-m-10-02.topic: Angles of shapes meeting around one point
z-m-10-02.goal: Using the fact that when vertices of shapes are gathered around one point, the angles must add up to one full turn (360°) for there to be no gap and no overlap, judge by comparing the size of the gap with one angle of a shape, and make several solutions yourself.
z-m-10-02.material: One angle of a regular triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon is 60°, 90°, and 120°, respectively. When you gather the vertices of several shapes at one point, if all the angles around that point add up to 360° (one full turn), they fit exactly with no gap and no overlap. If the sum is less than 360°, a gap is left, and if it is more than 360°, the shapes overlap. This task considers only "around one point", and does not consider whether a wide floor can be completely covered. No picture is shown.
z-m-10-02.thinking.0: Testing a claim using the size of angles
z-m-10-02.thinking.1: Making several solutions that fit the conditions
z-m-10-02.thinking.2: Explaining why the impossible cases are impossible
z-m-10-02.prereq.0: One full turn around a point is 360°
z-m-10-02.prereq.1: One angle of a regular triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon is 60°, 90°, and 120° respectively (given as data)
z-m-10-02.s.s1.prompt: Jimin gathered 3 squares and 1 regular triangle at one point and a gap of 30° was left. Jimin said, "If I put one more regular triangle, the gap will be filled exactly." Which judgment about this statement is correct?
z-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.0: Find out how much angle in all the 3 squares and 1 regular triangle take up around one point.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write the size of the remaining gap and the size of one angle of a regular triangle side by side and compare them.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.o.a: Right. A regular triangle is a small shape, so it fits in the gap.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.r.a: Even a small shape won't fit if one of its angles is bigger than the gap. You have to look at the size of one angle, not the size of the shape.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.o.b: Right. A gap is left, so putting one more of the same shape will fill it.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.r.b: The fact that there's a gap alone doesn't decide it. You have to compare the size of the gap with the size of one angle of the shape to be added.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.o.c: You can't tell. You can only check by actually putting it down.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.r.c: If you know the sizes of the angles, you can gather the angles and judge before putting anything down.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.o.d: Wrong. One angle of a regular triangle is 60°, which is bigger than the 30° gap.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that judged by comparing the size of the gap with one angle of the shape.
z-m-10-02.s.s1.explain: 3 squares are 90°×3=270°, and 1 regular triangle is 60°, so 330° is filled now and 30° remains. If you put another regular triangle, one angle is 60°, which is bigger than 30°, so it becomes 390° and overlaps. To fill the gap, you need a shape with one angle of 30°.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to gather a regular triangle (one angle 60°), a square (one angle 90°), and a regular hexagon (one angle 120°) at one point with no gap and no overlap. Mixing two or more kinds of the three shapes, find three ways with different numbers of shapes.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write one angle of each of the three shapes, decide the number of the shape with the biggest angle, and find the remaining angle.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether you can fill the remaining angle exactly with the other shapes, and if not, change the earlier number.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of shapes as a natural number that is 0 or more.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the angles around the point is 360°.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the angles is not 360°. Gather the angles and check whether a gap is left or they overlap.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.ok.c3: You mixed two or more kinds.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.fail.c3: You used only one kind of shape. Try mixing two or more kinds.
z-m-10-02.s.s2.explain: The ways to mix and make 360° are four, with (regular triangles, squares, regular hexagons) counts of (3, 2, 0), (4, 0, 1), (1, 2, 1), (2, 0, 2). For example, (1, 2, 1) is 60°+90°×2+120°=360°.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.prompt: One angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Can you fill the space around one point with only regular pentagons and no gap and no overlap? Use the sum of the angles for 3 and for 4 pentagons to judge, and write it.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the sum of the angles when you gather 3 regular pentagons and when you gather 4.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare each sum with the size of one full turn, and say whether a gap forms or they overlap.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you work out both the case of 3 and the case of 4?
z-m-10-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use whether the sum of the angles is less than or greater than 360° as your reason?
z-m-10-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is your conclusion of "so what happens" clear?
z-m-10-02.s.s3.model.0: 3 angles of 108° make 324°, which is less than 360°, so a gap of 36° is left, and 4 make 432°, which goes over 360°, so they overlap. So you can't fill it exactly with only regular pentagons.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.model.1: 108×3=324 and 108×4=432, so no number of them makes 360. So it doesn't work with only regular pentagons.
z-m-10-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer written only as expressions also has clear evidence.

z-m-10-03.title: How many diagonals does a polygon have?
z-m-10-03.topic: The rule for the number of diagonals of a polygon
z-m-10-03.goal: Experience how a guess made from little data gets fixed by new data, and connect the number of diagonals from one vertex to the total number of diagonals to check even the reason for the rule.
z-m-10-03.material: A diagonal is a line segment connecting two vertices of a polygon that are not next to each other. This task considers only polygons with no dents going inward. A quadrilateral has 4 sides, a pentagon has 5 sides, a hexagon has 6 sides, and a heptagon has 7 sides. No picture is shown, so feel free to draw them on paper yourself.
z-m-10-03.thinking.0: Guessing a rule from little data and testing it
z-m-10-03.thinking.1: Judging whether new data changes or strengthens a guess
z-m-10-03.thinking.2: Making several cases that fit the conditions
z-m-10-03.prereq.0: The meaning of a diagonal and the names quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-03.prereq.1: Writing the number of sides and the count side by side in a table to compare
z-m-10-03.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose your guess, and after seeing the new data, decide whether to keep your guess or fix it.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.0: If you can draw it, name the vertices, connect two points that are not next to each other, and record what you counted in a table.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether new data fits or contradicts the earlier guess; if it fits, add the reason, and if not, decide what to fix.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.info: A diagonal is a line segment connecting two vertices that are not next to each other. Only polygons with no dents going inward are considered. Name the vertices ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ and draw them yourself. When I drew and counted, a quadrilateral had 2 diagonals and a pentagon had 5 diagonals.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many diagonals do you think a hexagon, which hasn't been drawn yet, has?
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Both b and d are reasonable thoughts for now. With only two pieces of data, the guess that "it goes up by 3 each time" needs to be tested.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 10: found by multiplying the earlier two numbers, 2 and 5.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Nothing in the data gives a reason to trust the rule of multiplying the two numbers. Check whether the same method is right for the quadrilateral and the triangle too.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 8: it went up by 3, so it will probably go up by 3 again.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a guess that extended the rule found from two pieces of data. Whether this guess is right has to be tested by counting the hexagon directly.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 12: the hexagon has 6 sides, so it's 2 times the number of sides.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If you apply the same rule to the quadrilateral (4 sides, 2 diagonals), it doesn't fit the data.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It's hard to know for now: I want to draw the hexagon and count directly.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is the attitude of holding off on a guess when there is little data and wanting to check directly.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.info: I drew the hexagon and counted the diagonals, and there were 9. So far the quadrilateral has 2, the pentagon has 5, and the hexagon has 9.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many diagonals do you think a heptagon has?
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.after: c is the rule found from the data 2, 5, 9, and d is the attitude of wanting to check that rule. Both are reasonable. The first "3 at a time" doesn't fit the hexagon data, so it needs to be fixed.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 12: I think it keeps going up by 3 at a time.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The hexagon came out as 9, not 8. Check again whether the thought that it goes up by 3 at a time fits the current data.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 18: I think it will be 2 times the hexagon.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check whether it doubles between the quadrilateral and pentagon, and between the pentagon and hexagon too.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 14: the increases are 3, then 4, so the next goes up by 5.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a guess found by looking at how the increases changed in the data 2, 5, 9.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It's hard to know for now: I want to draw the heptagon and count directly.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is the attitude of making a guess but wanting to test it by checking directly.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.info: I counted the diagonals that can be drawn from one vertex: the quadrilateral has 1, the pentagon has 2, and the hexagon has 3. That's because you can't draw a diagonal to the vertex itself and to the 2 neighboring vertices on either side. A heptagon can have 4 drawn from each vertex. If you add up the numbers counted from all the vertices, each diagonal gets counted twice, once from each end point.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many diagonals does a heptagon have in all?
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.after: A heptagon has 14 diagonals. This is the same as the 14 guessed earlier from the rule, and now we also know why it is 14. The quadrilateral 4×1÷2=2, the pentagon 5×2÷2=5, and the hexagon 6×3÷2=9 are all right too.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 28: count 4 at each of the 7 vertices.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: That is the number counted twice, once from each end. Think about how to count each only once.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 14: add up all the counted numbers and divide by two.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is thinking that corrected counting the same diagonal twice and connected it to the 14 guessed earlier.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The data gives no reason to add. Try the same method on the quadrilateral (4+1) and check whether it matches 2.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 4: the number you can draw from one vertex.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Tell apart the number counted from one vertex and the total number counted from all vertices.
z-m-10-03.s.s1.reflect: The first "goes up by 3 at a time" was fixed by the hexagon data, and the 14 for the heptagon was confirmed both as a rule-based guess and by the reason. Tell apart which data changed the guess and which data strengthened it.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.prompt: For a polygon with n sides (no dents going inward, and n is a natural number from 3 to 12), find three different cases where the number of diagonals is greater than the number of sides.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of sides and the number of diagonals side by side for the quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.1: Widen the table to the right and check whether there are more diagonals than sides when there are 7 sides and 8 sides, too.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of sides as a natural number from 3 to 12.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of diagonals is greater than the number of sides.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of diagonals is not greater than the number of sides. Compare the number of diagonals and the number of sides side by side in a table for the quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon.
z-m-10-03.s.s2.explain: The pentagon has 5 sides and 5 diagonals, which is the same. From the hexagon (6 sides, 9 diagonals) on, there are more diagonals. Any of 6 to 12 is right.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.prompt: A polygon with no dents going inward has 10 diagonals that can be drawn from one vertex. How many sides does this polygon have?
z-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number of sides and the number of diagonals from one vertex side by side for the quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon, and look at the difference.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.1: Use the difference you found to decide the number of sides when there are 10 diagonals, and check again whether the same relationship holds for the quadrilateral.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.r.a: This is thinking that saw the number of diagonals from one vertex as the same as the number of sides. Check whether the two numbers are the same in the quadrilateral and the pentagon.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.r.b: This is the direction of subtracting 3 backward from 10. Check with the data whether the number of diagonals from one vertex goes up or down as the number of sides goes up.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.r.c: This is thinking that found the difference between the number of diagonals from one vertex and the number of sides and used it backward.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.r.d: This is thinking that saw the difference between the number of sides and the number of diagonals from one vertex as one bigger. Check whether you counted both the vertex itself and its two neighbors.
z-m-10-03.s.s3.explain: The number of diagonals that can be drawn from one vertex is (number of sides) − 3. If there are 10, the polygon has 13 sides, so it is a 13-gon. Then the total number of diagonals is 13×10÷2=65.

z-m-10-04.title: What has to be the same to be a regular polygon?
z-m-10-04.topic: Conditions for being a regular polygon (sides and angles)
z-m-10-04.goal: Test the claims "if the sides are equal" or "if the angles are equal, it's a regular polygon" with counterexamples, and explain that both conditions are needed to be a regular polygon.
z-m-10-04.material: A regular polygon is a polygon whose sides all have the same length and whose angles all have the same size. Only polygons with no dents going inward are considered. A rhombus is a quadrilateral whose four sides all have the same length, and a rectangle is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles. Two friends said this. Seoa: 'A polygon whose sides are all the same length is a regular polygon.' Roha: 'A polygon whose angles are all the same size is a regular polygon.' No picture is shown.
z-m-10-04.thinking.0: Judging whether claims are true or false and making counterexamples
z-m-10-04.thinking.1: Working out whether one condition or two are needed
z-m-10-04.prereq.0: The meaning of a regular polygon (a polygon whose sides are all the same length and whose angles are all the same size)
z-m-10-04.prereq.1: The meaning of a rhombus and a rectangle, and that the four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360° (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-04.s.s1.prompt: Seoa said, 'A polygon whose sides are all the same length is a regular polygon.' Which judgment about this statement is correct?
z-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.0: Read the meaning of a regular polygon again, and write the condition on the length of the sides and the condition on the size of the angles separately.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think of whether there is a quadrilateral made with all sides the same length but angles of different sizes.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.o.a: Wrong. A rhombus with angles of 60° and 120° has four equal sides.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that came up with a shape whose sides are all equal but whose angles are not, and used it as a counterexample.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. A regular polygon must have all its angles the same size too.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.r.b: This is a valid judgment based on the meaning of a regular polygon. It would be stronger if you showed that a shape with equal sides but different angles really exists.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.o.c: Right. If all the sides are equal, all the angles automatically become equal too.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.r.c: You have to check whether the angles automatically become equal just because the sides are equal. Look for a shape whose sides are equal but whose angles are different.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.o.d: Can't tell. We can't draw every polygon.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.r.d: To show something is wrong, even one counterexample is enough. You don't need to check every shape.
z-m-10-04.s.s1.explain: There are polygons whose sides are all equal but whose angles are not. For example, a rhombus with all four sides 5 cm and angles of 60°, 120°, 60°, 120° has all sides equal but is not a square, so it is not a regular polygon. Even one counterexample breaks "all".
z-m-10-04.s.s1.acc.0: This is a valid judgment based on the meaning of a regular polygon (the sides must be equal and the angles must be equal). It would be stronger if you showed one shape with equal sides but different angles.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.prompt: Let's make a counterexample that breaks Seoa's statement. In a rhombus whose four sides are all s cm, decide one angle p and the angle q next to it, and make two rhombuses of different shapes that are not squares. In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal and the four angles add up to 360°.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.0: If opposite angles are equal and the four angles add up to 360°, think about what relationship there is between the two neighboring angles p and q.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide p first, then fit q, and check that it is not a right angle.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The side length is greater than 0.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The side length must be greater than 0.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The two neighboring angles add up to 180°.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The two neighboring angles of a rhombus do not add up correctly. Use the fact that opposite angles are equal and the four angles add up to 360°.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c3: It is not a right angle, so it is not a square.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c3: If the angle is a right angle, it becomes a square. It must be a rhombus that is not a square.
z-m-10-04.s.s2.explain: For example, a rhombus with sides of 5 cm and angles of 60° and 120°, and a rhombus with angles of 70° and 110°, both have four equal sides but unequal angles, so they are not regular polygons. Count the same shape (a pair of the same angles) only once.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.prompt: Roha said, 'A polygon whose angles are all the same size is a regular polygon.' Write, giving one shape for each, why Seoa's statement and Roha's statement are each wrong, and write what conditions are needed to be a regular polygon.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.0: Look at which differs, the side lengths or the angle sizes, in the shape that breaks Seoa's statement.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.1: Decide on a shape that breaks Roha's statement, and compare what is the opposite of the earlier shape.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use a shape with equal sides but different angles for Seoa's statement, and a shape with equal angles but different sides for Roha's statement?
z-m-10-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the shapes concretely by name or numbers?
z-m-10-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write the conclusion that both conditions, sides and angles, are needed?
z-m-10-04.s.s3.model.0: A rhombus is the counterexample for Seoa's statement. Even though all four sides are equal at 5 cm, the angles are 60° and 120°, so it is not a regular polygon. A rectangle is the counterexample for Roha's statement. Even though all four angles are equal at 90°, it is 3 cm wide and 5 cm tall, so it is not a regular polygon. So both the side lengths and the angle sizes must be equal to be a regular polygon.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.model.1: You can draw a rhombus that has all equal sides but is not a square, and you can draw a rectangle that has all equal angles but is not a square. So a regular polygon needs equal sides and equal angles.
z-m-10-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer written only with the names of the shapes, with no numbers, is also good if the counterexample is clear.

z-m-10-05.title: Does the quick way to find the perimeter always work?
z-m-10-05.topic: Perimeter of shapes made of grid squares, and the limits of a handy method
z-m-10-05.goal: Test with examples in which shapes the handy method of finding a shape's perimeter from the perimeter of the rectangle around it is right and in which it is wrong, and explain the conditions in which it holds by the features of the shape.
z-m-10-05.material:
One grid square is a square with sides of 1 cm. The shapes below are made by joining grid squares side to side, and have no holes inside. The perimeter of a shape is the length of the whole outer boundary line, and it also includes the boundary of the parts dented inward. ■ is a square of the shape, □ is an empty square, and the rows are read from the top.
Shape 가: row 1 ■□ / row 2 ■□ / row 3 ■■
Shape 나: row 1 ■■■ / row 2 □■□
Shape 다: row 1 ■□■ / row 2 ■■■
Shape 라: row 1 □■□ / row 2 ■■■ / row 3 □■□
Shape 마: row 1 ■□■ / row 2 ■□■ / row 3 ■■■
Jiho: 'If you find the perimeter of the smallest rectangle that just wraps around the shape (fitted to the grid lines), it's the same as the perimeter of the shape. You can find it fast!' Harin: 'I count the 1 cm edges of the outer boundary one by one. It takes time, but it's sure.'
z-m-10-05.thinking.0: Testing a method with several examples
z-m-10-05.thinking.1: Finding the conditions it holds in and counterexamples
z-m-10-05.thinking.2: Making several shapes that fit the conditions
z-m-10-05.prereq.0: Knowing the perimeter from the length of the outer boundary line of a shape when one grid square is 1 cm (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-10-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the shapes for which the value found by Jiho's method (perimeter of the wrapping rectangle) is the same as the value counted by Harin's method (the actual perimeter).
z-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each shape, first write the number of squares across and the number of squares down of the smallest rectangle it fits in.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.1: For the outer boundary of each shape, count the 1 cm edges separately by direction: top, right, bottom, and left.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.r.a: If you missed shape 가: counting the short edges of the boundary gives 10 cm, and the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle (2 squares across, 3 squares down) is also 10 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.r.b: If you missed shape 나: the boundary is 10 cm, and the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle (3 squares across, 2 squares down) is also 10 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.r.c: If you chose shape 다: the wrapping rectangle is 3 squares across and 2 squares down, so its perimeter is 10 cm, but if you also count the walls and bottom of the notch in the middle, the actual perimeter is 12 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.r.d: If you missed shape 라: the boundary is 12 cm, and the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle (3 squares across, 3 squares down) is also 12 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.r.e: If you chose shape 마: the wrapping rectangle is 3 squares across and 3 squares down, so it is 12 cm, but the notch is deep, so the actual perimeter is 16 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s1.explain: The actual perimeter and the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle are 10 cm and 10 cm for shape 가, 10 cm and 10 cm for shape 나, 12 cm and 10 cm for shape 다, 12 cm and 12 cm for shape 라, and 16 cm and 12 cm for shape 마. The ones that are the same are 가, 나, and 라. In 다 and 마, which have a notch dented inward, Jiho's value is smaller than the actual one.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.prompt: Think of a shape that is a rectangle w squares wide and h squares tall, with a notch 1 square wide and d squares deep cut at one spot in the top row that is not at either end. The notch does not reach the bottom edge, and at least 1 row is left below. Shape 다 is the case (w=3, h=2, d=1), and shape 마 is the case (w=3, h=3, d=2). Find three shapes with different w, h, d whose outer boundary length (perimeter) is 18 cm.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the actual perimeters of shapes 다 and 마 side by side with the perimeter of the rectangle without a notch, and look at how the extra length is related to the depth of the notch.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.1: Pick w, h, d and count the perimeter directly; if it is more than 18 cm, reduce it, and if it is less, increase it, and adjust.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c1: They are natural numbers that can make the shape.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Write w as a natural number 3 or more, h as 2 or more, and d as 1 or more.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c2: At least 1 row is left below.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The notch reaches the bottom edge. The depth of the notch must be at least 1 less than the number of squares down.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The perimeter is not 18 cm. Compare the perimeters of shapes 다 and 마 with the perimeter of the rectangle without a notch.
z-m-10-05.s.s2.explain: If you cut a notch, the perimeter is the perimeter of the rectangle without a notch, 2×(w+h), plus the length of the two walls of the notch, 2×d. The cases with 18 cm are (w, h, d) = (3, 4, 2), (3, 5, 1), (4, 3, 2), (4, 4, 1), (5, 3, 1), (6, 2, 1).
z-m-10-05.s.s3.prompt: How is the shape different between the shapes where Jiho's method is right (가, 나, 라) and where it is not (다, 마)? Write in what kind of shape Jiho's value differs from the actual perimeter.
z-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the shapes 가, 나, 라 where it is right and 다, 마 where it is not, following their outlines.
z-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.1: In shapes 다 and 마, find where the lines are that are not in the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle.
z-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say how the shapes where it is right and the shapes where it is not differ?
z-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write how the actual perimeter differs because of that difference?
z-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use at least one shape name (가 to 마) in your explanation?
z-m-10-05.s.s3.model.0: If a shape bulges outward, Jiho's method is right, but if the middle is dented in like 다, it's wrong. The walls and bottom of the dented part are lengths that are not in the perimeter of the wrapping rectangle, so the actual perimeter is longer.
z-m-10-05.s.s3.model.1: For shapes with a notch, Jiho's method is different. 가, 나, and 라 have no dented parts, so the values are the same, and in 다 and 마, the actual perimeter is bigger because of the walls on both sides of the notch.
z-m-10-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer explained by 'has a notch / has no notch' is also good.

z-m-10-06.title: Angles you can and can't make with two set squares
z-m-10-06.topic: Making new angles by joining corner angles of set squares
z-m-10-06.goal: Sort out which angles can and can't be made from sums and differences of set square corner angles, make angles that fit the conditions yourself, and explain why the biggest obtuse angle is 150°.
z-m-10-06.material: The corner angles of set square 가 are 30°, 60°, and 90°, and the corner angles of set square 나 are 45°, 45°, and 90°. Suppose there are several of the same set squares. Without a protractor, you pick one corner angle from each of two set squares to make a new angle. Joining means placing the two angles side by side with their vertices together, and overlapping means laying one angle on top of another and looking at the angle that is left over. No picture is shown.
z-m-10-06.thinking.0: Sorting possible cases from impossible cases
z-m-10-06.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for the biggest case
z-m-10-06.prereq.0: The corner angles of the two kinds of set squares (30°·60°·90°, 45°·45°·90°)
z-m-10-06.prereq.1: The meaning of acute, right, and obtuse angles, and the size of angles when angles are joined or overlapped (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-06.s.s1.prompt: The corner angles of set square 가 are 30°, 60°, and 90°, and the corner angles of set square 나 are 45°, 45°, and 90°. Suppose there are several of the same set squares. Pick one corner angle from each of two set squares, and choose all the angles you can make by joining them with their vertices together or by laying one angle on another and taking the leftover angle.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.0: Among the corner angles 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°, pair them two at a time and write the angle made by joining each pair.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.1: For the same pairs, also write what angle is left if you lay the small angle on the big one, and compare with the choices.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.a: 80° is close to 75° or 90°, but you have to check one by one whether any of the sums and differences of the possible pairs is 80°.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.b: If you missed 15°: think of the way of making it with the leftover angle when you overlap (for example, the angle left when you take 45° from 60°).
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.c: 110° is close to 105° or 120°, but if you write all the possible pairs with none missing, there is no 110° among the sums and differences.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.d: If you missed 105°: it is an obtuse angle made by joining 60° and 45°. You can make angles bigger than 90° by joining too.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.e: If you missed 75°: it is the angle made by joining 30° and 45°.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.r.f: If you write all the sums or differences of the possible pairs, 100° doesn't come out. It looks like 90° plus 10°, but there is no corner angle of 10°.
z-m-10-06.s.s1.explain: From the corner angles 30, 45, 60, 90, joining two gives 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, 135, 150, 180°, and the leftover angles from overlapping are 15, 30, 45, 60°. So 15°, 75°, and 105° can be made, and 80°, 100°, and 110° cannot.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to make an obtuse angle (an angle greater than 90° and less than 180°) by joining two set square corner angles (one each from 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) with their vertices together. Find three cases where the size of the angle you make is different.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.0: From the four corner angles, write all the pairs of two and find the sum of each.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.1: Keep only the sums greater than 90° and less than 180°, and count the same size only once.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c1: x is a corner angle of a set square.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be one of the set square corner angles (30, 45, 60, 90).
z-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c2: y is a corner angle of a set square.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c2: y must be one of the set square corner angles (30, 45, 60, 90).
z-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c3: a is the size of the two angles joined together.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c3: a is not the size of the angle made by joining x and y.
z-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c4: a is not an obtuse angle (an angle greater than 90° and less than 180°).
z-m-10-06.s.s3.prompt: What is the biggest obtuse angle you can make by joining? Also write why you can't make a bigger obtuse angle. (180° is a straight line, so it is not an obtuse angle.)
z-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how best to choose the bigger of the two corner angles so that the joined angle is as big as possible.
z-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write the case with the two biggest angles joined and the next case, and compare them with the condition for an obtuse angle.
z-m-10-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The biggest obtuse angle is ...
z-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you link the reason there is no obtuse angle bigger than 150° with the biggest corner angle?
z-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what happens if you join 90° and 90°?
z-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare with another pair (for example, 45°+90°)?
z-m-10-06.s.s3.model.0: It is 150°. It is 90° and 60° joined. If you join 90° and 90°, you get 180°, a straight line, which is not an obtuse angle, and the next biggest corner angle is 60°, so 150° is the biggest.
z-m-10-06.s.s3.model.1: 150°. The biggest corner angle is 90°, but if both are 90° it becomes 180°, which doesn't work, so I use one 90° and the next biggest, 60°, to get 150°.

z-m-10-07.title: How many lines perpendicular to line 가 can you draw?
z-m-10-07.topic: The number and position of lines perpendicular to a line
z-m-10-07.goal: Learn that there are many lines perpendicular to a line, that a line becomes just one once you fix the one point it passes through, and explain, along with how to check, that this is the same even if that point is off the line.
z-m-10-07.material: On a sheet of paper there is a line 가 that is straight without end. If two lines meet and the angle they form is a right angle, the two lines are perpendicular to each other. If you put one side of the right-angle corner of a set square against the line and draw along the other side, you can draw a perpendicular line. Jiho and Seoyun are talking about perpendicular lines. No picture is shown, so draw one line on a sheet of paper and try it with a set square.
z-m-10-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-10-07.thinking.1: Examining the range of a claim (how many, in which cases)
z-m-10-07.prereq.0: A line (a straight line without end), a right angle, and the meaning of perpendicular
z-m-10-07.prereq.1: How to use the right-angle corner of a set square (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-07.s.s1.prompt: On a sheet of paper there is a line 가 that is straight without end. Choose all the correct statements about lines perpendicular to line 가.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put one side of the set square's right-angle corner against 가 and slide it a little at a time along 가 while drawing lines.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.hint.1: Fix a point ㅈ, and look at how many ways there are to place the set square so that you can draw a line through that point.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.o.a: There is only one line on the paper that is perpendicular to line 가.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.r.a: Put one side of the set square's right-angle corner against 가, slide it along 가, and draw perpendicular lines. How many can you draw?
z-m-10-07.s.s1.o.b: You can draw many lines perpendicular to line 가 by changing the position.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that found out that you can draw many perpendicular lines by sliding the set square along 가.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.o.c: If you fix a point ㅈ on line 가, there is only one line that passes through point ㅈ and is perpendicular to 가.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that found out that once you fix one point, the perpendicular line is decided as one.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.o.d: Lines perpendicular to line 가 will meet each other someday.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.r.d: Draw two perpendicular lines with the same set square, and look at whether the distance between the two lines changes.
z-m-10-07.s.s1.explain: If you slide the set square along 가 and draw, you can draw as many lines perpendicular to 가 as you like. But if you fix the one point it passes through, the perpendicular line through that point is decided as one. Lines perpendicular to 가 are in the same direction with respect to 가, so they never meet.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.prompt: Jiho asked Seoyun, 'Draw a line perpendicular to line 가 for me.' For Seoyun to draw exactly the same line Jiho has in mind, what should she ask Jiho to tell her in addition?
z-m-10-07.s.s2.hint.0: Divide into what you already know from the words 'perpendicular line' and what you don't know yet, and write them down.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.hint.1: Try one by one which piece of information, if you were told it, would decide the line as one.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.o.a: How many degrees the angle is that the line makes with 가
z-m-10-07.s.s2.r.a: The word 'perpendicular' already includes the information that it is a right angle (90°). Work out what you still don't know.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.o.b: Where the point is that the line passes through
z-m-10-07.s.s2.r.b: This is thinking that found out that a position is needed to decide one line.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.o.c: How many cm long that line is
z-m-10-07.s.s2.r.c: A line is straight without end, so it can't be described by length. Tell apart a line segment from a line.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.o.d: How many cm long line 가 is
z-m-10-07.s.s2.r.d: 가 is also a line without end, so it has no length, and it can't decide the position of the perpendicular line.
z-m-10-07.s.s2.explain: The word perpendicular already includes the direction (90° with 가). So if she knows just one more point it passes through, the line is decided as one. A line is straight without end, so you can't tell lines apart by length.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.prompt: Seoyun said, 'If point ㅈ is not on line 가 but outside 가, you can't draw a line through point ㅈ that is perpendicular to 가.' Decide whether this is right, and write how you could check with a set square or by paper folding.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.hint.0: Suppose point ㅈ is outside 가, and put one side of the set square's right-angle corner against 가.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.hint.1: Slide the set square along 가 and see whether there is a time when the other side touches point ㅈ.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state clearly whether you can draw it or not?
z-m-10-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write concretely about the set square's right-angle corner or the folding method?
z-m-10-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you include a way to make it pass through point ㅈ?
z-m-10-07.s.s3.model.0: You can draw it. Put one side of the set square's right-angle corner against 가, and slide it along 가 until the other side touches point ㅈ, then draw.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.model.1: You can draw a perpendicular line even through a point ㅈ outside 가. Fold the paper so that 가 lies on top of itself, but make the fold line pass through point ㅈ, and a right angle forms.
z-m-10-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: Checking by folding is good too.

z-m-10-08.title: How can we say that opposite angles are equal?
z-m-10-08.topic: The relationship among the four angles formed when two lines meet
z-m-10-08.goal: Understand that a few values measured with a protractor can't guarantee "always", derive that opposite angles are equal from the fact that a straight line is 180°, and explain it in easy words to a younger sibling who can't use a protractor.
z-m-10-08.material: Two lines meet at a point ㅇ and make four angles. Call these angles ㉮, ㉯, ㉰, ㉱ going clockwise. ㉮ and ㉰ face each other, and ㉯ and ㉱ also face each other. Two neighboring angles, for example ㉮ and ㉯, put together make one line, a straight angle (180°). Harin measured ㉮ as 50° and ㉰ as 50° and said, 'Opposite angles are always equal.' Geonu measured ㉮ as 70° and ㉰ as 69° on another pair of lines and said, 'Sometimes opposite angles are different.' No picture is shown.
z-m-10-08.thinking.0: Examining the limits of measurement as evidence
z-m-10-08.thinking.1: Deriving one fact from given facts
z-m-10-08.thinking.2: Changing an explanation to suit the listener
z-m-10-08.prereq.0: That a straight angle is 180°, and measuring angles with a protractor (Grade 4 level)
z-m-10-08.prereq.1: That two lines meeting make four angles
z-m-10-08.s.s1.prompt: Harin measured ㉮ as 50° and ㉰ as 50° with a protractor. Geonu measured ㉮ as 70° and ㉰ as 69° on another pair of lines. When reading the protractor's scale, you can be off by about 1°. Which is the best evaluation of the two friends' measurements?
z-m-10-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write down how many pairs Harin measured and how many Geonu measured, and how much of an error can come from reading the scale.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check each friend's conclusion one by one against two standards: 'shapes not measured' and 'error'.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.o.a: Geonu got 70° and 69°, so there are cases where opposite angles are different.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.r.a: You can't tell whether a 1° difference is really a different size or an error from reading the scale.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.o.b: Harin's measurement was the same both times, so it's fine to say opposite angles are always equal.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.r.b: If only one pair was measured, you can't guarantee "always". There are still shapes not measured.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.o.c: If you use a protractor very many times, "always equal" is proven perfectly.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.r.c: Measuring a lot makes you trust it more, but it doesn't guarantee that there is no shape you haven't measured.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.o.d: Measurements can be off a little, so you can't decide "always equal" from measurement alone.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that knows the limits of measurement and tries to find evidence other than measurement.
z-m-10-08.s.s1.explain: No matter how many values measured with a protractor you collect, they can't guarantee "always", and you can't tell whether a 1° difference is really different or a reading error. So you need to try explaining with evidence other than measurement (the fact that a straight line is 180°).
z-m-10-08.s.s2.prompt: Decide the four angles ㉮, ㉯, ㉰, ㉱ so that neighboring angles put together make a straight line (180°). Make ㉮ an acute angle less than 90°, and find three cases where the size of ㉮ is different.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.hint.0: Decide ㉮ first, then decide the neighboring angle ㉯ that makes a straight line with ㉮.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.hint.1: Decide ㉯, ㉰, and ㉱ in order, checking that each makes a straight line with its neighbor, and at the end put ㉮ and ㉰ side by side and compare them.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.ok.c1: ㉮ is an acute angle and all four angles are greater than 0°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.fail.c1: ㉮ must be greater than 0° and less than 90°, and all four angles must be greater than 0°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of ㉮ and ㉯ is not 180°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of ㉯ and ㉰ is not 180°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum of ㉰ and ㉱ is not 180°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.fail.c5: The sum of ㉱ and ㉮ is not 180°.
z-m-10-08.s.s2.explain: If you follow all four sentences, ㉮=㉰ and ㉯=㉱ come out automatically. For example, if ㉮ is 30°, then ㉯=150°, ㉰=30°, and ㉱=150°. However you decided ㉮, ㉰ became the same as ㉮.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.prompt: A 3rd-grade younger sibling who can't use a protractor yet asked, 'Why are the opposite angles ㉮ and ㉰ always the same size?' The sibling knows that a straight line is 180°. Explain in easy words, without a protractor.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.hint.0: Find which angle makes a straight line with ㉮, and which angle makes a straight line with ㉰, and write each.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.hint.1: Look for an angle that appears in both cases, and say how that angle connects the two angles.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If you put ㉮ and ㉯ together, ...
z-m-10-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use "a straight line is 180°", which the sibling also knows, as the evidence?
z-m-10-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that ㉮ and ㉰ both make a straight line with the same angle ㉯?
z-m-10-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain with a reason, without saying to measure with a protractor?
z-m-10-08.s.s3.model.0: If you put ㉮ and ㉯ together, it's a straight line, so 180°. If you put ㉯ and ㉰ together, it's a straight line too, so 180°. ㉮ and ㉰ both make 180° when put together with ㉯, so they are the same size.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.model.1: The opposite angles ㉮ and ㉰ both join with the same angle ㉯ to make a straight line of 180°. Since adding to the same angle gives the same 180°, ㉮ and ㉰ are exactly the same size.
z-m-10-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer written as '180° minus ㉯' is good too.
